newsitem.title: USA: California orders temporary halt to redwood logging.
newsitem.headline: California orders temporary halt to redwood logging.

text.p: California officials ordered a temporary halt to the logging of fallen trees in an ancient redwood forest Wednesday because lumber workers broke the rules by cutting down a standing tree.
But a proposal backed by environmentalists to block so-called "salvage logging" in the old-growth redwood groves failed before a state board.

Environmentalists have for years fought to preserve Headwaters grove, the nation's largest privately-owned ancient redwood forest, and five other old-growth redwood groves near Eureka, 300 miles (500 kms) north of San Francisco.

A tentative agreement hammered out last month between California, the U.S. government and forest owner MAXXAM Inc set aside Headwaters and one other grove for parks, in return for $380 million in cash and land and a promise to smoothe environmental problems. It placed a moratorium on salvage logging in those two groves.

But Pacific Lumber Co, a MAXXAM subsidiary, still has a permit to cut 10 percent of dead, dying or diseased timber in the four other old-growth groves and it began the salvage logging Monday, angering environmentalists and some government officials who said it could endanger the agreement.

About 20 environmental activists from the Earth First group sneaked into All Species Grove, one of the ancient groves where salvage logging began, Tuesday pledging to confront loggers, according to published reports.

The California Department of Forestry said Wednesday it had ordered Pacific Lumber temporarily to halt salvage logging because it had cut down a standing tree in All Species Grove, violating conditions set in its salvage logging permit.
"The stop order will remain in effect until the department is confident that Pacific Lumber will operate within the conditions of its exemption," the department said.
State forestry officials planned to meet with Pacific Lumber employees to go over terms of the permit and salvage logging could resume as early as Thursday, officials said.
The California Department of Forestry also gave Pacific Lumber a citation for felling the tree, officials said.
Pacific Lumber Co spokeswoman Mary Bullwinkel said a bulldozer operator accidentally knocked down a small tree while dragging logs from the forest and then had to remove it.

A bid by environmental groups to halt the salvage logging on the grounds that more environmental review was required failed amid controversy at a meeting of the California Board of Forestry in Mount Shasta, northern California, Wednesday.
The board voted 4-2 in favour of a proposal to require lumber companies to go through a review process before they could salvage logs in an old-growth redwood forest.

But the board's legal experts ruled that five votes -- a majority of the nine-member board -- were needed to pass the proposal. Two members of the board recused themselves from the vote and one seat is vacant.

Cecelia Lanman, programme director for the Environmental Protection Information Centre, an environmental group fighting to preserve the ancient forests, said environmentalists believed four votes were enough to pass the proposal. "We're going to look into taking legal action on it," she said.
Pacific Lumber praised the board's decision to sustain its right to pick up dead trees as "just and fair."
The board did ask a committee to begin a review next month of procedures for salvage logging in old-growth forests.
